content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"Across the blind responses, the dominant identification of 'Hell' is the final place or state of divine punishment for the unrepentant after judgment — classically eternal conscious torment and separation from God, symbolized by fire, darkness, and the undying worm. Alternatives noted include metaphorical-fire traditionalism, annihilationism/conditional immortality (minority), universal reconciliation (minority), a this-worldly/existential reading (minority), and a lexical distinction reading in which English 'hell' conflates Sheol/Hades, Gehenna, and Tartarus (common in scholarship, but presented as an alternative, not the consensus core).","book_summary":"The book denies that 'hell' names one thing at all: it is a single English word laid over two distinct referents — Sheol/Hades, the grave that receives righteous and wicked alike (no punitive content), and Gehenna, a judgment that destroys. It explicitly flags 'eternal conscious punishment and separation from God' as merely the common teaching, and its phrase 'the judgment that destroys' signals an annihilationist reading of Gehenna rather than everlasting conscious torment.","consensus_core_identification":"Hell = the final postmortem state/place of divine punishment for the unredeemed, dominantly understood as eternal, conscious torment and separation from God.","book_core_identification":"'Hell' = a translation artifact covering two different referents: (1) Sheol/Hades, the common grave of all the dead, and (2) Gehenna, a final judgment whose outcome is destruction (not everlasting conscious torment); the doctrine depends on which underlying word is present.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book reclassifies the Sheol/Hades passages (e.g., Ps 16:10) out of the punishment category entirely — they refer to the grave that swallows righteous and wicked alike — while restricting judgment language to Gehenna passages. Within the retained Gehenna set, it further reclassifies the outcome from eternal conscious torment to destruction (Matt 10:28).","material_contradiction":"The consensus core asserts a single referent whose nature is eternal conscious punishment and separation from God. The book asserts (a) there is no single referent — 'hell' is two different things — and (b) the judgment component (Gehenna) destroys rather than eternally torments. 'Eternal conscious torment' and 'judgment that destroys' cannot both be true of the same referent in the same sense; the book explicitly brackets the consensus view as merely 'commonly taught.'","rationale":"Although the book's position stitches together two views the consensus responses list as alternatives (the Sheol/Hades–Gehenna lexical distinction, rated common, and annihilationism, rated minority), the classification compares the book's core against the consensus's core identification, which across three of four responses is eternal conscious punishment. Accepting the book requires rejecting that identification twice over: it denies the unified referent ('one English word laid over two different things') and replaces everlasting torment with destruction. This is replacement of the central identification, not a mere boundary adjustment, so DIVERGENT rather than REFINED. It is not NOVEL because both components are recognizable in the consensus's listed alternatives.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue REFINED: the consensus responses themselves list the Sheol/Gehenna distinction as a 'common' scholarly alternative and annihilationism as a notable minority, and Response C even denies settled consensus on duration and nature of punishment. On that framing, the book preserves the general category (divine judgment on the wicked via Gehenna) and merely refines the term's semantics and outcome, disaggregating rather than contradicting.","confidence":"medium"}
